title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch had seen nothing striking or improper in the fact that his wife had been sitting with Vronsky at a separate table, in eager conversation with him about something. But he noticed that to the rest of the party it appeared striking and improper, and for that reason it seemed improper to him as well. He made up his mind that he must speak to his wife about it.

On reaching home, Alexey Alexandrovitch went to his study, as he usually did, sat down in his low chair, opened a book on the Papacy to the place where he had laid the paper-knife in it, and read until one o'clock, just as he usually did. But from time to time he rubbed his high forehead and shook his head, as though to drive away something. At his usual time he got up and got ready for bed. Anna Arkadyevna had not yet come in. With a book under his arm he went upstairs. But this evening, instead of his usual thoughts and meditations on official details, his thoughts were absorbed by his wife and something unpleasant connected with her. Contrary to his usual habit, he did not get into bed but fell to walking up and down the rooms with his hands clasped behind his back. He could not go to bed, feeling it was absolutely necessary for him first to think thoroughly through the situation that had just arisen.

When Alexey Alexandrovitch had decided he had to talk to his wife about it, it had seemed a very easy and simple thing. But now, as he began to think over the question that had just arisen, it appeared very complicated and difficult.

Alexey Alexandrovitch was not a jealous man. Jealousy according to his notions was an insult to one's wife, and one ought to have confidence in one's wife. Why one ought to have confidence — that is, complete conviction that his young wife would always love him — he did not ask himself. But he had no experience of a lack of confidence, because he had confidence in her, and told himself that he ought to. Now, although his conviction that jealousy was a shameful feeling and that one ought to feel confidence had not broken down, he felt that he was standing face to face with something illogical and irrational, and did not know what to do. Alexey Alexandrovitch was standing face to face with life — with the possibility of his wife loving someone other than himself — and this seemed to him very irrational and incomprehensible, because it was life itself. All his life Alexey Alexandrovitch had lived and worked in official spheres, having to do with the reflection of life. And every time he had stumbled against life itself he had shrunk from it. Now he felt something akin to what a man might feel who, while calmly crossing a chasm by a bridge, suddenly discovers that the bridge is broken, and that there is a chasm below. That chasm was life itself; the bridge was the artificial life in which Alexey Alexandrovitch had been living. For the first time the question of the possibility of his wife's loving someone else presented itself to him, and he was horrified at it.

He did not undress, but walked up and down with his regular tread over the resounding parquet of the dining-room — where one lamp was burning — over the carpet of the dark drawing-room, where the light was reflected on the big new portrait of himself hanging over the sofa, and across her boudoir, where two candles were burning, lighting up the portraits of her parents and women friends and the pretty knick-knacks on her writing-table that he knew so well. He walked across her boudoir to the bedroom door and turned back again. At each turn in his walk, especially on the parquet of the lit dining-room, he halted and said to himself, "Yes, I must decide this and put a stop to it; I must express my view of it and my decision." And he turned back again. "But express what — what decision?" he asked himself in the drawing-room, and could find no reply. "But after all," he asked himself before turning into the boudoir, "what has happened? Nothing. She talked a long while with him. But what of that? Surely women in society can talk to whom they please. And then, jealousy lowers both me and her," he told himself as he went into her boudoir; but this dictum, which had always carried such weight with him before, now had no weight and no meaning at all. And from the bedroom door he turned back again; but as he entered the dark drawing-room some inner voice told him that this was not so, and that if others had noticed it, that showed there was something. And he said to himself again in the dining-room, "Yes, I must decide and put a stop to it, and express my view of it..." And again at the turn in the drawing-room he asked himself, "Decide how?" And again he asked himself, "What has happened?" and answered, "Nothing," and reminded himself that jealousy was a feeling insulting to his wife; but again in the drawing-room he was convinced that something had happened. His thoughts, like his body, went round a complete circle without coming upon anything new. He noticed this, rubbed his forehead, and sat down in her boudoir.

There, looking at her table with the malachite blotting case lying on top and an unfinished letter, his thoughts suddenly shifted. He began to think of her, of what she was thinking and feeling. For the first time he pictured to himself vividly her personal life, her ideas, her wishes, and the idea that she could and should have a separate life of her own struck him as so alarming that he hurried to dispel it. It was the chasm he was afraid to peer into. To put himself, in thought and feeling, in another person's place was a spiritual exercise not natural to Alexey Alexandrovitch. He regarded this spiritual exercise as a harmful and dangerous abuse of the imagination.

"And the worst of it all," he thought, "is that just now, at the very moment when my great work is approaching completion" (he was thinking of the project he was putting forward at that time), "when I need all my mental peace and all my energy, just now this stupid worry has to fall on me. But what's to be done? I'm not one of those men who submit to uneasiness and worry without having the strength of character to face them."
"I must think it over, come to a decision, and put it out of my mind," he said aloud.

"The question of her feelings, of what has happened and may be happening in her soul, is not my affair; that's the affair of her conscience and falls under the head of religion," he said to himself, taking consolation in the sense that he had found the division of regulating principles under which this new circumstance properly belonged.

"And so," Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself, "questions about her feelings and so on are questions for her conscience, with which I can have nothing to do. My duty is clearly defined. As the head of the family, I am the person bound in duty to guide her, and so, in part, the person responsible; I am bound to point out the danger I see, to warn her — even to use my authority. I must speak plainly to her." And everything he would say tonight to his wife took clear shape in Alexey Alexandrovitch's head. Thinking over what he would say, he somewhat regretted that he should have to use his time and mental powers for domestic consumption, with so little to show for it; but in spite of that, the form and content of the speech before him shaped itself as clearly and distinctly in his head as a ministerial report.

"I must lay out fully the following points: first, the value to be attached to public opinion and to decorum; secondly, the religious significance of marriage; thirdly, if need be, the calamity that may follow for our son; fourthly, the unhappiness likely to result for herself." And, interlacing his fingers, Alexey Alexandrovitch stretched them, and the joints cracked. This trick, a bad habit — the cracking of his fingers — always soothed him, and gave precision to his thoughts, which he so badly needed now.
There was the sound of a carriage driving up to the front door. Alexey Alexandrovitch halted in the middle of the room.

A woman's step was heard climbing the stairs. Alexey Alexandrovitch, his speech at the ready, stood with his crossed fingers pressed together, waiting to see whether another crack would come. One joint cracked.
Already from the sound of light steps on the stairs he could tell she was close, and though pleased with his speech, he felt frightened of the explanation that lay ahead of him...
